passage:
I'm Vasudha, and I was hanging washing on the terrace when I saw my neighbour's daughter Elizabeth lying flat on her roof with a blanket, staring up. It was a clear night after the power cut, with stars everywhere. She didn't move for a long while.
When I whispered across and asked what she was doing, she said, "Just looking." Then, "It's so big, Aunty. It makes me feel tiny, but in a nice way." She was smiling.
Earlier that evening she had fretted loudly about a spelling test, and now she never mentioned it. I can't say exactly what she was thinking. I left her the quiet and went in.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth lie on the roof with?
qa.a: Elizabeth was lying flat on her roof with a blanket.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel as she looks at the stars?
qa.a: Tiny but happy. She says the sky is so big it makes her feel small in a nice way, and she is smiling.

qa.q: What did Vasudha choose to do when she saw Elizabeth?
qa.a: Vasudha whispered one question, listened, and then left Elizabeth alone with the sky instead of talking more.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see Elizabeth's stargazing?
qa.a: Vasudha notices the smile and that the spelling test worry has vanished, but admits she cannot say exactly what Elizabeth is thinking.

grounding: A child under a night sky feels small yet happy, and awe softens her earlier worry, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Saturday. On the ferry across the wide river, Mohit stopped chattering. The far bank was a thin line and the water went on and on. His mother Salma asked if he was cold. "No," he said, holding the rail. "It's just so big."
Monday. At school he tried to tell a friend and got stuck for words. He drew the river across a whole page and left the boat as a tiny dot.
The next Saturday. Back on the ferry, Mohit stood quietly again. This time he grinned at Salma and said, "I feel small, but happy small." He did not ask for her phone once.

qa.q: What did Mohit draw at school on Monday?
qa.a: He drew the river across a whole page, with the boat as a tiny dot.

qa.q: What is Mohit feeling on the ferry, and how does he describe it the next Saturday?
qa.a: He is awed and quiet at first, then says he feels small but happy small.

qa.q: What did Mohit choose to do at school to share his awe?
qa.a: He drew the river across a whole page with a tiny boat when words failed him.

qa.q: What might Salma notice about Mohit between the two Saturdays?
qa.a: She may notice he is calmer and more thoughtful, since he stays quiet at the rail and does not ask for her phone.

grounding: A child looking at a huge river feels small yet happy, and awe expands his sense of the world.

passage:
Mehak, you're sulking about the school race? Let me tell you something. When I was nine, I lost the running race at our school sports day in front of the whole village, and I cried all the way home. That evening my Baba took me on the ferry across the Brahmaputra.
In the middle, the river was so wide I couldn't properly see either bank, only water and a red sun sinking into it. The fishing boats looked like seeds. I remember feeling tiny, like a speck. And strangely, so happy. The race suddenly seemed like a very small thing on a very big river.
I held Baba's hand and didn't say a word the whole way. Your Anirban Dadu still thinks of that ferry whenever something feels too big.

qa.q: Which river did Anirban cross on the ferry?
qa.a: The Brahmaputra.

qa.q: How did young Anirban feel in the middle of the river?
qa.a: Anirban felt tiny, like a speck, yet strangely happy, and the lost race stopped mattering.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Anirban after the race?
qa.a: Baba taking him on the ferry that evening, letting the huge river shrink the disappointment without any talk.

qa.q: Why might Baba have taken Anirban on the ferry that evening?
qa.a: Baba perhaps hoped the wide river would comfort his tearful son better than words could.

grounding: Shows a child on a vast river feeling small yet happy, with a disappointment softening in the face of it.

passage:
The school trip to the hill fort went wrong from the start. The bus was an hour late, it drizzled all the way up, and Sonali left her new water bottle on the bus seat. At the top there was only thick white fog. She sat on the wall and sulked.
"Wait," said Imran Sir, the geography teacher. "Give it five minutes."
Then the wind moved. The fog tore open like a curtain, and there was the whole valley: green fields, a silver river twisting for miles, tiny villages, cloud shadows sliding over them.
Sonali forgot to breathe. She felt smaller than a stone on that wall, and a warm happiness spread through her chest. The bottle didn't matter at all. She stood beside Imran Sir in silence until the fog closed again.

qa.q: What did Sonali leave on the bus?
qa.a: Her new water bottle, on the bus seat.

qa.q: What did Sonali feel when the fog tore open?
qa.a: Sonali felt tiny but warmly happy, full of awe, and the lost bottle stopped mattering.

qa.q: What did Imran Sir do that helped Sonali see the view?
qa.a: He asked her to give it five minutes instead of giving up, and then stood beside her in silence.

qa.q: How might Imran Sir have felt when the fog cleared?
qa.a: He was probably glad and moved too, having waited for it and sharing the silence with Sonali.

grounding: Shows a child before a vast valley feeling small yet strangely happy, with her own worries fading.

passage:
Raghav had been grumbling all evening about his spelling test, so his aunt Hansa took him for a walk along Marine Drive in Mumbai. The sea was dark and endless, the waves hitting the tetrapods with a huge hush. Lights curved away along the shore like a necklace, and far out on the water a tiny ship's light blinked.
Raghav climbed onto the wall and stared. "Masi, how far does it go?"
"All the way to other countries."
He was quiet for a long time. The wind pushed his hair back. "I feel like an ant," he said, and then laughed, a surprised, happy laugh.
On the way home he held her hand and talked about ships, not spelling.

qa.q: What did Raghav say he felt like?
qa.a: An ant.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel looking at the sea?
qa.a: Raghav felt small, like an ant, but surprisingly happy, laughing a happy laugh.

qa.q: Why might the walk have helped with Raghav's grumbling?
qa.a: The vast sea pulled his attention away from the spelling test, and he talked about ships instead.

qa.q: What might Hansa have noticed on the way home?
qa.a: Hansa likely noticed he was calmer and more cheerful, holding her hand and chatting about ships.

grounding: Shows a child facing the vast sea at night feeling small yet happy, his self-focus softening.

passage:
"Saurabh Chacha, why did the lights go off in the whole village?"
"Power cut, Yogesh. Come up to the roof. Bring the mat."
"It's so dark. I can't see anything."
"Wait. Lie down. Look up."
"...Chacha."
"Hmm?"
"There are SO many. Were they always there?"
"Always. The city lights hide them."
"That white smudge, is that a cloud?"
"That's our galaxy. Millions of stars."
"Millions? Then... we're really, really small."
"Very small."
"It's weird. I feel tiny, but I feel happy. Is that allowed?"
"It's allowed."
"I was so angry about losing the match today. It doesn't feel big anymore."
"Things look different from up here, na?"
"Can we stay till the power comes back? Even if it takes all night?"
"Till you fall asleep, Yogesh."

qa.q: What did Chacha say the white smudge was?
qa.a: Chacha said, "That's our galaxy. Millions of stars."

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling while looking at the sky?
qa.a: Yogesh felt tiny but happy, full of wonder at so many stars, and puzzled that both feelings could exist together.

qa.q: Why did the lost match stop feeling big?
qa.a: Seeing how vast the sky was made Yogesh's own worry seem smaller, so the anger softened.

qa.q: How might Chacha have felt lying on the roof with Yogesh?
qa.a: Chacha likely felt calm and warm, enjoying Yogesh's wonder and happy to stay until Yogesh fell asleep.

grounding: A child under a night sky feels small yet strangely happy, and awe softens anger about a lost match.
